speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: asked the Minister for Education how are schools helping students who are bullied to restore their confidence and rebuild their identity and self-worth.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: asked the Minister for Education (a) what specific criteria are used to determine whether an incident is to be classified as bullying that warrants action to be taken by the educational institution; (b) whether the Ministry has conducted any recent surveys among students to assess the prevalence of bullying in schools; and (c) what are the interventions and support provided to teachers to help them deal with bullying cases in the course of their work.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: asked the Minister for Education (a) whether the Ministry has observed a rising trend in bullying cases involving school students; and (b) how can the Ministry better prevent bullying of school students and support victims of bullying.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: asked the Minister for Education (a) in the last five years, what are the observed trends relating to the number of bullying cases schools have received; (b) what is the breakdown between online and offline bullying incidents reported to schools; and (c) whether there are any special guidelines given or approaches taken for cases of bullying involving students with neurodiverse conditions or disabilities and, if so, what are they.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: My response will also cover related questions from Ms Hazel Poa, Mr Sharael Taha, Mr Gan Thiam Poh and Assoc Prof Jamus Lim, which are scheduled for subsequent Sittings.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Minister, I think you mentioned Question No 28.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The Ministry of Education (MOE) takes a serious view of all forms of hurtful behaviour, from once-off insensitive remarks to more persistent, intentional acts of bullying and even physical violence.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Schools and IHLs have rules and regulations which prohibit any form of bullying.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Our schools and IHLs educate students against these negative behaviours and work with families, the community and partners to intervene promptly and address them.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Members Ms Hany Soh, Mr Gerald Giam, Mr Louis Chua asked about the trends in bullying incidents.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In the last five years, the average number of bullying incidents has remained steady.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Members Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim and Dr Wan Rizal asked about how MOE educates our students and equips them to deal with threats of bullying.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: From young, students learn pro-social behaviours through lessons and role-modelling.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Through the Character and Citizenship Education (CCE) curriculum and a school environment that emphasises values and respect, students acquire skills to be kind to their classmates, resolve disagreements respectfully and stand up against bullying.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Students learn what to do when they encounter unsafe situations.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Stay calm, do not retaliate, but move away and seek help from adults nearby, and alert their teachers and parents.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Through cyber wellness lessons, students learn to be respectful and responsible users online.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Whether online or offline, they should report any incident of bullying to their teachers or School Leaders.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: As students sometimes prefer to turn to their friends for support, schools have established peer support networks and trained students to help and look out for one another, and in conflict management.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: These educative efforts continue in our IHLs, which raise awareness about anti-bullying through modules teaching respect and appropriate behaviour, as well as peer support structures.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Members Mr Yip Hon Weng, Ms Hazel Poa, Mr Christopher de Souza and others asked about the intervention and support for bullying victims and perpetrators, and how schools collaborate with families, community partners and Police to address them.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Teachers are trained to create a positive classroom culture, recognise distressed students, and proactively address hurtful behaviours and bullying.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: All pre-service teachers receive this training, and new teachers are supported by experienced staff and school counsellors.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In-service teachers also receive refresher training as part of their professional development.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: When any incident of bullying within or outside schools is reported, schools and IHLs conduct thorough investigations before deciding on the appropriate course of action.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We adopt a tiered approach based on the severity of incident.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In cases arising from careless remarks and misunderstandings, teachers guide students to resolve their differences and reach a common understanding.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For cases involving persistent, intentional acts of bullying, serious disciplinary actions are taken in addition to the restorative actions.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For cyber bullying incidents, schools guide students to report these to the online service provider.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: When schools and IHLs come to know of any incident of severe bullying or fights, they work closely with parents and the authorities to ensure students' well-being and safety.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: They also mete out the necessary disciplinary consequences and guide students to change their thinking and behaviours so that they can learn to be responsible members of the community.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Similarly, our schools and IHLs consider the seriousness of the incident and take into consideration the profile and needs of the students involved, when taking disciplinary actions.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Schools may put perpetrators on detention or even suspend them from attending lessons.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Whenever a student is affected by bullying, whether as a victim or perpetrator, the teachers and school counsellors provide emotional support to help the student cope and mend relationships.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Students who continue to be distressed will be referred to community resources such as the Response, Early Intervention and Assessment in Community mental Health (REACH) teams for more specialised support.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The objective of these educative and restorative efforts is to help students learn from their mistakes.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: These efforts are taken to turn the bully around, rather than just "expelling" or suspending them from school.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: When relationships are affected due to conflicts and misconduct, schools and institutions take steps to educate, discipline and restore relationships in the school community, and these efforts require parents' support and partnership.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Parental guidance and partnerships are vital in shaping children's character.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Parents guide their children by role-modelling positive behaviour and interaction with others.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: When a child faces bullying, parents are encouraged to remain calm and provide emotional support, reinforcing pro-social values and coping skills.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Similarly, when a child has bullied someone, parents can guide their child to learn from the mistake, apologise sincerely and make amends.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: As mending relationships and improving behaviour require time and practice, parents are encouraged to collaborate closely with schools to address the situation effectively.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: When students witness bullying incidents, they are reminded not to record and share the incidents online to avoid further hurting the parties involved.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Similarly, when videos become viral, everyone should exercise care in responding to them.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The bullying perpetrators often also need help to turn over a new leaf.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: As a society, we must be careful not to normalise such behaviours unintentionally.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Let us stand together to discourage copycats and attempts to out-viral the last bullying video.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: With your help to monitor community and online spaces to keep our students safe and to stop bullying incidents among students when you witness them, we will be that village that raises our children well.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It requires a nuanced approach that carefully considers the well-being and reform of both victims and perpetrators.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: While it is reassuring to hear the efforts that we have made to equip teachers in schools with the tools to manage bullying, the recent cases of both physical and psychological bullying highlight the need for us to have continuous evaluation.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The long-lasting emotional impact on victims is vital to ensure schools have adequate resources to address these challenges effectively.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Furthermore, the detection and reporting processes must remain robust to prevent unreported cases from escalating.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Over the years, I have seen students who have been bullied, but they are afraid to come forward, simply because of the retaliation.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: With that, I would like to ask the following supplementary questions.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And finally, what are some considerations that the Ministry would take before anti-bullying policies are being reviewed to ensure continued relevance and effectiveness?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: First, I do not think there is an easy or simple, and certainly, we do not want simplistic, way to measure the effectiveness of our measures.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Ultimately, the test of the pudding is, do our students feel safe in school, do our students feel that they have a good school environment where they can interact with their peers with respect?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Second, on the ratio of counsellors, as I have mentioned in my speech and before, we allocate the number of counsellors based on the following considerations.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: There are some schools with higher needs and we will reinforce them with the necessary numbers.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Third, it does not mean that we depend only on counsellors.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: All teachers are trained to a certain extent and we work in partnership with the community and the teachers.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: On the third supplementary question about when we will review the policies, we constantly review the policies and we apply the measures according to the needs of the respective schools as well.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I believe the monitoring and surveillance is important to pick out early indications, telltale signs that there are situations of bullying.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: And so, I would like to ask the Minister in terms of resourcing for the schools, whether the schools are equipped or resourced enough to be able to do that monitoring and surveillance.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Also, given that the cases now are increasingly more complex and with the workload of the teachers as well, one would really have to step up resources to be able to reduce the cases of bullying.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: On the second point, Mr Liang Eng Hwa says that issues are becoming much more complex.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Part of it is that, today, we live in a hyperconnected world.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Students have access to many things on the Internet, relationships are becoming much more complex, not just between and amongst students, but relationships and expectations are also becoming much more complex with parents.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, if I can point out something: when students have issues, we try to mend the relationships, guide the students on the positive trajectory.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Very often, we will also need the partnership of the parents and, sometimes, in very unfortunate circumstances, the adults can also be a complicating factor when children quarrel.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Will MOE consider implementing nationwide school programmes that encourage and guide students who witness bullying to not just be bystanders, but upstanders, where students learn ways to identify, intervene and support peers who are being bullied and report the bullying?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This could shift the peer culture by making it clear to the bullies that they do not have the approval of their peers and assuring the victims that they are not alone.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: On the second supplementary question, there are, indeed, baseline policies, but when we say that we intervene, I would just like to reiterate what I have spelt out clearly in my response just now.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, these are complex issues, as Mr Liang Eng Hwa says, and it is important for us not to oversimplify these issues.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Very often, the rehabilitation for both the victim and perpetrators is not a short journey and we need to put in the necessary efforts with the parents and the community partners in order to do this well.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While the criteria for bullying classification seem clear, are there concerns about under-reporting of bullying cases?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: There can also be over-reporting of a different kind.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Because, as mentioned, this issue is a complex one.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: There will also be cases where people have experienced uncomfortable situations which may not exactly constitute "bullying", but they will also raise this to the adults or parents and we will take actions as necessary.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, it is not just about having more channels.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The channels are there for us to use.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But regardless of the channels, we want to give people and students the confidence that if you are in doubt, where you feel troubled, you should be able to use the existing channels to report it to the adults and then have the adults work with the students to see how they can mend the relationships and move the relationships forward.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, as many other Members have shared, I am concerned that the number of reported cases, though steady over the past few years, may not be indicative of the underlying concerns that many parents have.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: So, two points, if the Minister can help us to understand.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: These are not just about having more channels.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But how has MOE enhanced the detection and reporting of bullying cases over the years?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: One, students today are exposed to much more diverse influences beyond schools, beyond the community and even beyond the families, and largely through the Internet.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, the sources of information and the kind of exposures that they are being exposed to have become much more complex.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Second, on the positive side, we have also stepped up efforts to sensitise our students to what constitutes bullying and that can also help us to have better detection.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And students today are much more confident, willing and able to come forward and tell us what they have experienced.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: On the other hand, we also have students who are becoming much more sensitive, not just sensitised, to some of these issues and what they perceive as bullying may or may not correspond to what other people may perceive as bullying.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But regardless of the complexities, we encourage all students to report instances when they feel they have not been treated with respect or they have felt unsafe, to let the school leaders know.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We will work with the parents and the community to try and rehabilitate the perpetrators and also to take care of the physical and emotional needs of our children.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, how has this changed over the years?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Well, besides those points that I mentioned, today, when such instances happen in schools, very often we have to not just manage the issues between the students; sometimes, we also have to manage the issues amongst the parents and their great expectations on all parties of what the other side should do.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I do not think I heard the Minister answering them.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The first being for a breakdown between the offline and online bullying incidents that are reported to schools.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And part (c), relating to whether there are any special guidelines, given our approaches taken for cases of bullying involving students with neurodiverse conditions or disabilities, and if there are such guidelines, what are they?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And it is important, especially for this last point, because different measured strategies need to be behind how these students are handled, because they need to be sensitive or also effective, and not all teachers or counsellors might feel that they are able to handle some of the more complex issues.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But as Members have noted, this could also be because people are less sensitised to what constitutes online bullying.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, for example, if a child views that he or she has been excluded from a group repeatedly, persistently, does that constitute a form of psychological bullying?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: On the second point about neurodiversity, that is why we handle all cases sensitively.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It is not a one-size-fits-all method to handle things.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Some children with special needs may have, advertently or inadvertently, caused harm to others and they may not know and, when we counsel them, we have to handle them with care because of their different needs.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: On the other hand, when students with special needs are bullied or made to feel uncomfortable, we will also have to make special efforts to counsel the perpetrators.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Minister mentioned just now that the trend of bullying in the past five years has remained steady.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As trends for social behaviours may take some time, this five-year timeframe may not be sufficient.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Does the Minister have figures over a longer timeframe like, for example, 20 years?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I have already explained that in the last few years, the data has been relatively stable.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: That is about the only change that we have done recently.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: On the second issue that Ms Hazel Poa mentioned, this is exactly the point, because it is not about focusing on just the bullying, but the potential causes of why people engage in such behaviours, whether is it children or adults or teenagers, and there are many reasons for this.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I think the literature has various hypotheses on this.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But for more recent events, one of the things that we watch closely is the impact of the COVID-19 safe distancing measures and the reduction in opportunities for our children to grow up interacting with people, as they would have done previously, and whether this would have an impact on the kind of social or anti-social behaviours that they have.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The second thing that we are watching very closely is what is happening on the Internet.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Sometimes, even though the numbers are the same, the virality of some of these instances will then spawn copycats or attempts to "out-viral" the last known instance.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: That is why when we respond to such instances, we have to be very careful to not aggravate the situation.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These videos may cause further embarrassment to the victims of the bullying.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In fact, in the past one week, another video of students engaging in public displays of affection has come up.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: So, is there any possibility that the Ministry can work together with the Ministry of Digital Development and Information (MDDI) to get social media platforms to remove such videos, so that we remove the embarrassment for these students?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We are particularly concerned when videos of such instances go around because, as I have mentioned, they can have consequences.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: One, it can lead to more copycat attempts.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Because we need to give the perpetrators a chance to rehabilitate.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I have received many letters, emails from concerned parents.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And I am not sure it will help us in our rehabilitation efforts.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Imagine a young child doing something wrong and it is on record forever.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This is not to make an excuse for the people who have done wrong, the perpetrators.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For the people who have done wrong, we try to rehabilitate them, just as we punish them for doing wrong.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: That is why, in the last sentence in my reply, "True justice must blend punishment with rehabilitation." And the last thing I hope we do not get into is where adults jump in and complicate the situation.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Sometimes, these are most unhelpful in helping us to manage the situation on hand when we rehabilitate the perpetrator and help the victim to heal.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, I would like to just make an appeal for all of us to be careful.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Then there are also letters and suggestions that we throw the children out of school.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Again, I am not very sure that helps the children in the long term.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I have also parents who have written to me to say, "Can you please do not suspend my child from going to school because when they are not in school, they are in a much more difficult environment where they do not have anybody to guide them even".

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, I think we need to help the victim to heal.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We also need to rehabilitate the perpetrators to the extent that we can.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But, of course, at the end of the day, nobody is above the law, and, in the extreme cases, the full force of the law will be applied to the perpetrators.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To be clear, I understand that parents cannot be held completely liable for the actions of their children, which is a step that some jurisdictions like France or Germany actually have in place.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: That said, I am concerned when there is limited or no parental involvement at all.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I have Sengkang parents who have explained that even after they have reached out to the school and to the discipline master, the actions have been somewhat inadequate in their view because of insufficient involvement on the family side of the perpetrator, to be clear.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I understand that in the UK, parents may face orders to attend counselling or even face fines.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While MOE may not wish to go as far, I wonder if there are merits to having this sort of joint counselling sessions, keeping in mind as the Minister said, that we do want to be very sensitive to adult involvement, but here, I feel it is about building a relationship between the parent of the perpetrator and the child.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Indeed, we get the parents of the perpetrators involved because we believe that this is part of the rehabilitation process.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And if you have cases where you think the parents of the perpetrator would like to get involved more, but is not adequately provided for, let us know and we will follow up on this.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Most of the time, it is the other way around, where we would like to engage the perpetrators' parents to get their support and cooperation, but sometimes this may not be forthcoming.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: On the other hand, the Member has touched on the other point about expectations.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Sometimes, we have difficult cases when parents take things into their own hands and this is certainly most unhelpful because that will be a negative role modelling of what we want for our children.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: There appears to be a movement, as there are repeat instances of such pages.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Usually, it is "xxx", the school name, confidential.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: What is MOE doing to equip schools on dealing with such pages and what measures can students and parents take with the school, MDDI and the Singapore Police Force to take down these chats and pages?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Can the community work with MOE on rehabilitation, like what the Minister had spoken about?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Doxxing, itself, in certain contexts, will constitute bullying as well.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I am not confident that this is top of mind for them, but we will certainly try to get their help, especially when the physical and psychological well-being of our children are at stake.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And I hope the platform companies will work with us, MDDI and the Police to manage some of these issues.
